new_statements.quote: Надо полагать, что многие из этих явлений объясняются действием ударения, которое не может, разумеется, считаться полностью исследованным. В словах, заимствованных из таджикского, ударение сохраняется на последнем слоге (pâšâ 'падишах', ixtiyar 'воля', 'выбор' и т. д.); в двусложных причастных формах прошедшего времени ударение падает иногда на корневой слог (giyo 'пошел', kiyo 'сказал'), [в] трехсложных причастных формах ощущается помимо главного и второстепенное ударение: langáyò 'насадил', bagáyò 'бросил'. На односложные послелоги (-a, -na, -ko, -ta) ударение не падает. В двусложных послелогах ударение падает обычно на второй слог (-matá, -nalá, -pačá, -kulá и т. д.). Во всех случаях надо иметь в виду, что, хотя ударение здесь и силовое, оно неизмеримо более слабое, чем, скажем, в русском языке, и потому в записях носителем русского языка всегда возможны ошибки.
new_statements.translation: One must suppose that many of these phenomena [reductions in connected speech] are explained by the action of stress, which cannot, of course, be considered fully investigated. In words borrowed from Tajik the stress is kept on the last syllable (pâšâ 'padishah', ixtiyar 'will, choice', etc.); in disyllabic past-participle forms the stress sometimes falls on the root syllable (giyo 'went', kiyo 'said'); in trisyllabic participial forms a secondary stress is felt besides the main one: langáyò 'planted', bagáyò 'threw'. Monosyllabic postpositions (-a, -na, -ko, -ta) do not take stress. In disyllabic postpositions the stress usually falls on the second syllable (-matá, -nalá, -pačá, -kulá, etc.). In all cases one must bear in mind that, although the stress here is dynamic, it is immeasurably weaker than, say, in Russian, and therefore errors are always possible in recordings made by a native speaker of Russian.

new_statements.translation_language: Russian (assembled from overlapping OCR snippets; diacritics on pâšâ/bagáyò and the postposition list partly OCR-garbled in the raw snippets)
new_statements.rule_in_words: No blanket rule is stated. What Oranskij commits to: weak dynamic (expiratory) stress; Tajik loanwords retain word-final stress; native disyllabic past participles are only 'sometimes' root-(initial-)stressed, implying final stress otherwise (giyó); trisyllabic participles carry main stress on the medial (stem-final) syllable with a secondary stress on the final vowel (langáyò); disyllabic postpositions are end-stressed, monosyllabic ones unstressed; an example bâzár ~ me bázər-a giyo shows stress moving in connected speech. Everything points to a predominantly word-final (right-edge) stress, but the author explicitly calls the question under-investigated, and the 2011 Jazyki mira summary by Zograf & Oranskaia omits stress altogether and raises the possibility of tone — hence 'unclear' rather than 'fixed-final'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Trisyllabic participial forms have a secondary stress on the final syllable besides the main stress (langáyò 'planted', bagáyò 'threw').
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllabic past participles sometimes root-stressed (gíyo, kíyo); monosyllabic postpositions never stressed; stress shifts/reductions in connected speech (bâzár vs. me bázər-a giyo); recordings by a Russian ear may err because the stress is weak.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level remarks drawn from text recordings (folklore dictation, Hissar valley speakers, 1950s-60s); the passage sits in a discussion of reduction at word junctures in connected speech, so citation-form vs. phrase behaviour is not separated. Zograf & Oranskaia 2011 additionally flag a possible tonal compensation for lost aspiration (uninvestigated).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Parya of the Hissar (Gissar) valley, Tajik SSR / Surkhandarya (Uzbek SSR) = Glottolog pary1242 [paq] (other names: Afghon, Laghmani, parya-sazi; Tiwari 1970 calls the same lect 'Tajuzbeki'). Not to be confused with 'Parya Bhilali' (a Bhilali [bhi] variety in Madhya Pradesh) that appears in SIL survey titles.
